167.q: Yeah. He was just 50. You hit it. He's working up north.

167.t: Mezz Mezzrow as leader and his habits
167.s: Mezzrow called the session; Bunn got along with him but disliked his pot habit, which made Mezz sloppy and unreliable.
167.ch: Leo Watson and the Panassie sessions
167.q: And that's what used to bring us all down in the band, far as that's concerned, because Mezz didn't have his instrument punctual.

167.t: Drinking and nerves among performers; Leo throws things from the window
167.s: Bunn says performers drank to face the stage, with stage fright; Leo got drunk on gin and threw things out a seventh-floor window.
167.q: Well, it's pressures, yeah. When a man knows that he's got to go and do a set, he gets full of that whiskey, to hold the night out.

167.t: Feeding the broke band; pot smoking and the fight with Doug
167.s: Bunn passed the hat to feed the band, who smoked pot all night, and he split Doug's tiple in a fight in Buffalo.
167.ch: Spirits of Rhythm and the road in the 1930s
167.q: I'd get dates and go on and play and then nights when I didn't have to do nothing, I wanted to have some money, and the band got broke and everything, and I was around there feeding them.

167.s: Leo had a good attitude but drank heavily after reaching California, slept in Bunn's house with melting ice cream, and loved dressing well.
167.ch: Leo Watson and the Panassie sessions
167.q: And got to drinking heavy. And that's what kept it up -- he kept it up, and he'd go down and bum downtown, and he'd bum. I mean, just -- whenever he got feeling high and wanted to lay down, he'd go lay down, period. Leo -- right in my house -- not here, but in one of the houses I had, Leo used to…

167.t: The Lyons Brothers bring the Spirits west; the marijuana bust and quitting pot
167.s: The Lyons brothers took the Spirits from the Hickory House to Hollywood where all were jailed 45 days over one joint; Bunn quit pot afterward.
167.q: Working at the Hickory House. He come all the way from here to New York after this group, the Spirits of Rhythm, and brought us back here.

69.t: Who drank in the band and Harry Carney's driving
69.s: Early on only Sonny Greer and Otto drank; later others did, and Willard describes Carney driving Duke at high speed.
69.ch: Band personalities, Duke's last years and the office
69.q: It's a wonder he didn't get in to an accident driving Duke somewhere on the road to different towns, and after the dances, because he'd want to go to town, and they told me that Harry would really step on the gas, too.

69.t: Toby Hardwick and the superstition over thirteen musicians
69.s: Toby liked whiskey and had asthma; Willard recalls Lawrence Brown waiting because Duke wouldn't have 13 men.
69.ch: Band personalities, Duke's last years and the office

69.t: Disagreements with Duke over drug use in the band
69.s: He argued with Duke about men using drugs, citing Willie Cook playing nothing on stage and Paul Gonsalves sleeping on stage.
69.ch: Harry James, Bellson and the return to Duke
69.q: Well, I disagreed with him a lot of times -- the department in the band, about certain guys with the dope business, you know? Because I say, 'If ever the band come in here, well, I'm gonna tell who is using the dope in the band. I ain't going to jail.' Oh, he couldn't take that; he wouldn't see…

69.t: Reviving Willie Cook from an overdose in Canada
69.s: He and Procope rescued Willie Cook after an overdose, walking him with coffee; Cook later thanked him, and Tizol deplores the drug problems.
69.q: That was when we were in Canada. Some woman called and said that [Willie] (Jimmy) Cook was in there on the floor, and she was scared, because I think he knocked himself out, you know? With one of those shots. You see, so she asked if one of us could come and get him and do something about him,…

69.t: Tricky Sam, Whetsol, Freddie Guy and Sonny Greer
69.s: Short remarks on Tricky Sam's whiskey, Whetsol's nerves and decline, and Fred Guy's and Sonny Greer's arguments with Duke.
69.ch: On the road with Duke and his bandmates
69.q: What he was like? Tricky was a hell of a nice fellow. Only he liked his whiskey, you know, and when he got full of whiskey, you didn't know what he was gonna play! But he was a nice fellow, very nice.

69.s: A cigarette stub was found by Carney; Duke vouched for him at the 600 Club and Tizol had to show a birth certificate.
69.ch: Band personalities, Duke's last years and the office
69.q: happened once going in to Canada on the train. Whereabouts in Canada was it? Oh, I don't know what place it was -- Montreal, or Toronto; I guess it was one of those places, and they stopped the train one place, and we didn't know what was happening, and all of a sudden a bunch of men came in to our…

115.t: Cootie as bandleader; Gator Tail Jackson
115.s: Cootie blew every set, drank, and was choosy about drummers; Gus named tenor Willis Jackson 'Gator Tail'.
115.ch: Postwar: Chicago, Vinson, Hines and Cootie
115.q: We had a tenor player with us, and I can't think of his name, either. But he didn't work out too well, so we got Gator tail Jackson, from Florida.

115.t: Yank Lawson, Bob Haggart and Ed Hall
115.s: He found Yank Lawson drinks but is good-natured, Bob Haggart is sober, and Ed Hall had just died when he joined.
115.ch: World's Greatest Jazz Band and Denver
115.q: Offer him a drink. He doesn't know how to say no. But he's a nice guy. He's like Mr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde. He gets drunk and that's -- his big problem is his drinking. But he's a great guy.

115.s: Jay was the band's only heavy drinker; Gus got him up and showered him for work, and Jay called Gus 'W.W.'
115.q: I used to have to take him to work and put him in the tub there, because I stayed in the same house he stayed in. And I could have been staying home in Kansas, but I stayed in Missouri.

115.t: Getting drunk on the job once, in protest
115.s: Gus got drunk to match the band, threw up behind the bass and covered with a story about bad food; he never drank on the job again.
115.ch: Kansas City, Omaha and Lloyd Hunter
115.q: But they just got on my nerves. I couldn't take it, see. So -- but I got even. I got drunk one night. I'm playing the bass, and so I said, 'They going to get drunk, I'm going to get drunk with them.' And we played this town in Nebraska. And it was in a dance hall, see. We was playing dances, anyway.

115.t: Dating, a broken engagement and his drinking
115.s: At twenty he almost married in Kansas City, broke off the engagement and left for Omaha; he did not use drugs and drank bourbon moderately.
115.ch: Kansas City, Omaha and Lloyd Hunter
115.q: I was tied up in the music. I'd see other guys light up, and -- no, not for me. That wasn't for me, see.

115.t: Firing Lloyd Hunter after the Pipestone gig
115.s: At Pipestone, Minnesota the band got drunk on spiked ice water, and the angry young Gus fired leader Lloyd Hunter.
115.ch: Kansas City, Omaha and Lloyd Hunter
115.q: Like, as we were talking about that, I was playing bass in the band. And we left and went to Pipestone, Minnesota. I think that was Minnesota. Yeah, it was, Pipestone, Minnesota.

131.t: Drugs and drinking and how they affect playing
131.s: He compares pot, cocaine and alcohol and how booze makes him play looser.
131.ch: Maynard Ferguson and the drinking life
131.q: Influence of what? I play differently when I’m drinking than when I’m not drinking. But pot, I’ve lost interest. I mean I smoked so much pot it was unbelievable. But I’m not so interested in that anymore. That paranoia feeling has kind of left me. Marching powder — Peruvian marching powder, also…

131.t: Why booze and drugs go with jazz
131.s: Time on buses and in clubs; drinking as an occupational hazard.
131.ch: Maynard Ferguson and the drinking life
131.q: Somebody once said that the only time a musician should drink is while he works, or when he’s working. But you’ve got so much time. You work four hours a day. I mean I hate to say work, play, because I’ve never worked a day in my life. But I mean you’re basically playing but I mean when you’re on…

131.s: A drinking bet with the Ferguson band about a club he never played, ending in twenty shots on the bandstand.
131.ch: Maynard Ferguson and the drinking life
131.q: Oh yeah. One time we were playing with Maynard’s band and, oh that was a drinking band I mean it was just everything. But we were going to play at a place called the Beeches, which you know up there.

131.t: Drinking to forget, being fired for quitting, Vine Street
131.s: He recalls his wet and dry seasons and the day O'Day fired a pianist for quitting drinking.
131.q: The fact that I drink. That was actually from “The Little Prince.” When he went to see the tippler. He said, “why do you drink so much?” He says, I drink because I’m — whatever it was, “I drink to forget.” “Forget what?” “Forget that I’m ashamed.” “You’re ashamed of what?” “That I drink.” So it’s a…

131.s: Anita O'Day asks for him after Michael's Pub, he tours Europe and Japan and records at Vine Street, and they become drinking partners.
131.q: For some reason she came in to the picture because it’s a Gene Krupa legend. They were trying to — I call it “humping the grave.” They just keep trying to hump the grave you know. So now like here is Anita O’Day playing at Michael’s Pub in New York. And I had worked with her with the Buddy Rich…

143.t: Jackie McLean, Sonny Rollins and avoiding junkies
143.s: He lived near McLean and Rollins but kept his distance from addicts.
143.q: Yeah. I lived up there. I lived on 155th. He lived on 158th. Sonny Rollins lived around the corner. Edgecombe Avenue. I’d see all of them. But these guys were junkies. They were junkies. Sorry to say, but I had no use for no junkies. Because I thought it would just be my luck to be talking to one…

143.t: Staying friendly with difficult people: Monk, Miles, Elmo Hope
143.s: He relates how he kept friendships while avoiding junkies, with stories about Elmo Hope's car and the stolen hubcaps.
143.q: Oh, yeah. I’m an amazing guy, because I’m the only guy... Say, like, a guy like Miles... Miles did some bad things to people. He never did it to me. Any time I talked to him, he’d come up and we’d talk. Monk. Monk would hardly talk to people. People asked Monk, said, “How you doing, Monk?” He’d…

143.t: First organ on the road with John Patton, and Grant Green
143.s: Patton was his first road organist; he never took the addicted Grant Green on the road.
143.q: I don’t know how I met John. It was in New York. I met John Patton, Ben Dixon and Grant Green. We had a nice group. Nice group. I met Grant in East St. Louis, Illinois. In fact, I’m the one who brought him to New York.

143.t: Onyx Club visit and doubts about the scene
143.s: He found J.J., Stitt, Bud Powell and Miles playing well but in bad condition, and decided he could not handle that scene.
143.q: I went by the Onyx Club, too, to see my favorites. And very depressing. Heh-heh. The Onyx Club. That was on 52nd Street, too. They had J.J. and Sonny Stitt, Bud Powell, Miles, and every one of them was all messed up. It was terrible. Very depressing.

143.t: Walking away from Blue Note after a session with junkies
143.s: Angry over drug use at Rudy's house, he refused to record for two years.
143.ch: Hiatus, Blues Walk and the road
143.q: I really shouldn’t tell you this, because I’m going to put it in my book. I got mad at Blue Note Records. Angry. Because I went out to do a session one time at Rudy’s house, and we played a couple of tunes, and then some guy came by with some vitamins, and all of them went in the bathroom—Rudy,…

80.t: Fats's serious side: drinking rules and arriving at the studio steady
80.s: Fats told the band they could drink as they liked but must be able to play or they had fired themselves; he partied all night yet reached the 8 a.m. sessions with steady hands.
80.q: Very. Very. Oh, oh heck yeah, I mean when it came to business, and music, oh man, you -- you never met a man more serious in your life. Never. And, with all our drinking, and bottles he used to buy, and all that business, he'd tell you, said 'now don't get drunk. If you get drunk you fire yourself.…

80.t: Charlie Shavers, whose aunt he dated, and the fatherly advice
80.s: Autrey dated Charlie Shavers's aunt before knowing the boy was a trumpeter, was stunned to hear him on radio, and later warned him off drugs and traded choruses with him at the Stuyvesant Casino.
80.q: well -- I don't know. I knew Charlie from a kid, and I felt like a father to him, because I used to go around with Charlie's aunt, you know? And that's another story. I must tell you.

80.t: Stuff Smith's mental breakdown in Moline, and Autrey handling the band's money
80.s: In Moline, Illinois, Stuff, drinking rum and Cokes and spending the band's money, lost his mind; Autrey had been put in charge of paying the band by Joe Glaser.
80.ch: Hopkins, the South and Stuff Smith
80.q: You've heard of it. Well I was with -- there with Stuff, and we come out California and Chicago, and that business, and Stuff took ill. He was -- well, I would say that he was -- he lost his mind, or he was losing his mind, or -- I'm trying to think of a nicer way -- you know, I'm trying to think…

80.t: The suitcase bar for dry states
80.s: Fats carried a case of liquor for towns in dry states like West Virginia where nothing could be bought.
80.q: Well yes, because a lot of places we went to, I think in West Virginia places, dry states, you know, a lot of -- they didn't sell anything. So if he didn't carry it, you didn't have anything to drink.

80.t: Fats's eating and drinking, and treating the band as family
80.s: Fats ate and drank lavishly, bought for everyone and treated the band like family, remembering everybody's drink.
80.q: Well, I know. I know. I know. Fats drank, yes. Fats paid for it. He drank, but he paid for what he drank, and I think Fats ate well, doggone well. Fats ate the best of steaks, the best of this. He'd always -- get me a steak, and diced tomatoes, and this and that and the other, and he would eat damn…

17.s: Kirchner raises 'Dream About Reefers' and 'You'se a Viper'; Cole recalls the sidemen.
17.ch: Stuff Smith, 52nd Street and session work
17.q: Yeah, the rest of them Mack Walker, Bobby Bennett and Clyde Hart, wasn't it, or Sherman.

17.t: Don Byas in New York and later years
17.ch: Own groups, bebop and Savoy sessions
17.q: sit down there and liable to cause something else, and in this place nobody knows Don Bias, and they care less who Don Bias is really. And he's got his money out, about $800, $900 on him, in one of these big long pocketbooks and had it flashing out his back pocket." I said, "Don, things aren't like…

17.ch: Broadway, tenors, Billie Holiday and Rhythm Club memories
17.q: one of the first ones he called when he was there making some records with, what the devil is his name, for Dan Morgan.....

17.ch: Broadway, tenors, Billie Holiday and Rhythm Club memories
17.q: No I didn't. I didn't see Hawk all the time that he was growing a beard. I didn't see the Hawk. I know that one time we were all by to see Shorty Baker, he was at the Alvin Hotel and we all stopped by to see him, he wasn't feeling too well.

17.ch: Broadway, tenors, Billie Holiday and Rhythm Club memories
17.q: Roy, we made all his records with Billie Holiday together. Roy, Benny Goodman, Ben, Teddy Wilson, Kirby. We made the first records, 'Miss Brown to You,' 'What a Little Moonlight Can Do.' Roy was on those. Then I made so many records with Roy, 'Braggin' In Brass,' all those things. Roy, Charlie…

117.t: Why Tough drank: dipsomania versus musicians' lives
117.s: Dance asks what drove Tough to drink; Freeman says musicians don't drink because they are musicians, and Tough and Bix were dipsomaniacs.
117.q: Well, with all due respect to your question about the drinking, don't you think, Helen, that it doesn't really matter much what a person is, men don't drink because they are musicians.

117.t: Drink as escape for Tough; Freeman's hangovers
117.s: Freeman thinks Tough never enjoyed drinking but used it to escape tension, and describes his own horror of hangovers.
117.q: But, I think, to get back to your question, what made Dave drink. I don't think that Dave ever enjoyed drinking. It drove him crazy, but it was a way of escape for him, because he was so bright.

117.s: Freeman distinguishes a dipsomaniac from a drunkard, says Tough could not handle one drink, and wonders whether childhood shapes later life.
117.q: A dipsomaniac is a man who can smell a cork and go completely berserk. Dave Tough was not a big drinker. He would take one drink and he was gone, out of his mind. But let's --

117.t: His father's view of drink and Freeman's own health habits
117.s: Freeman's athletic father disapproved of Tough's and McPartland's drinking; Freeman and his brother kept to health, golf and moderation.
117.q: When I say we are all sick, I think that I was very much influenced and frightened by my father who was an athletic man, and thought it was a thought it was a sin to drink sin to destroy oneself. He loved Dave Tuft and Jimmy Tough McPartland. They were at our home all the time, but he

117.t: Dave Tough, Hemingway and young musicians who drank
117.s: Tough went to Oak Park High, introduced Freeman to Hemingway, and like Wettling and Condon began drinking young; Benny Goodman turned pro at twelve.
117.q: And, incidentally, Dave Tough was one of the first people I ever heard speak about Hemingway. He idolized Hemingway and I remember that six months after

566.t: Musicians who need a drink to work: Jay McShann
566.s: Humes grows disgusted when Jay McShann gets drinking, though he still plays wonderfully. Dance laments how many musicians harm themselves this way.
566.ch: Europe and the Black and Blue years
566.q: Well, I don't know, sometimes it seems like a lot of them can't work unless they have a little taste. Because sometimes I get disgusted with Jay. As well as he plays. And then when he gets to drinking he don't know what the hell you singing.(laughter)

566.t: Scott Hamilton and the night he drank at her gig in New Orleans
566.s: Humes admires young Scott Hamilton but scolded him about drinking. In New Orleans he drank through a televised fight, reeled on the stand, apologised and promised it would not happen again.
566.ch: Europe and the Black and Blue years
566.q: of the great ones. He's young, and everybody respect s him. And he's coming up and he's doing big things, you know. But honey he would get so high he wouldn't know how to put his horn in his mouth, and I used to talk to him. And I'd say, Scotty, it's sad because you've got such a future, and you're…

566.t: Copying the old lifestyle: a young singer imitating Billie Holiday's drinking
566.s: Dance says Hamilton copied the 1930s lifestyle. Humes tells a young woman singer who fell off a bar stool and said 'Billie Holiday drank' that she need not pattern herself on Billie; Benny Goodman gave that singer her start.
566.ch: Europe and the Black and Blue years
566.q: You know, a lot of them feel like a little friend of his come telling me. She get up there and she drank and fell off the bar stool and . . .

566.t: Her pianist Jerry and his stage seizures
566.s: Her current pianist Jerry stopped drinking on doctor's orders. She describes a concert in Chicago where he stopped playing, and says he has something like seizures.
566.q: And I know when we were in Chicago and I'm standing up there just singing and Jerry just stopped playing and I'm standing by the piano and I say, 'what's the matter? What's the matter?' And he says, 'what you singing'. And then he starts playing and he played in another key and I don't know what…

566.t: Jimmy Rowles: a favourite pianist who drinks
566.s: Rowles is one of her favourite pianists, though he drinks despite saying he does not. He now plays for Ella, and walked out on Alberta Hunter at the Cookery during intermission.
566.q: But poor Jimmy, he said, 'Helen you know I don't drink no more. We got to work together'. I said, 'you don't drink no more?' So I went down to hear him one night and here he was, he drank about two gallons of beer. I said, we'll that's just as bad as that fire-water.

169.t: Drugs in Korea and Rudy's overdose
169.s: Rudy buys unreliable drugs and nearly dies.
169.q: : Well, Rudy wanted to get high all the time, man. And over there you can get the drugs, but you know, it wasn't very nice, because you didn't ever know what you was getting. You might have been here today and gone tomorrow, according to what the things were. Like a little kid would walk up to you:…

169.s: Fats gave him a speedball; later cocaine laced with heroin left him with a habit.
169.q: Well, I came here once from California when I was living out there, when Bird was out there, and I came here. And I ran into Fat Girl, and he turned me on, you know, with a speedball. That's the first time I'd ever heard about it. I didn't even know what a speedball was. Shit, I hung out with him…

169.t: Neighbours on 45th Street; being Number One but unemployed
169.s: Everyone around him used drugs while he was out of work.
169.q: Like, Miles and all the guys used to come by my pad. I used to live on 45th Street, and in fact, everybody and his brother came by and said, "Hey, Maggie, can I use your bathroom?" I said, "Well, yeah..."

169.t: Why so many musicians got hooked
169.s: Idleness and easy availability; a neighbour dealer got him started.
169.q: : Yeah, in order to get you started. The guy living right across the street from me used to come by and say, 'How you feel, Maggie?' I said, 'Well, I don't feel so good.' And he said, 'Well, come on, hang out with me,' and

169.t: The 1957 bust, Rikers Island, and Woody Herman
169.s: He served four months, then joined Woody Herman's small band and was struck on the chops.
169.q: : Yeah, I got busted, and I went to Riker's Island for four months. And I did that, and when I came out then I cleaned up. Then I got a gig with Woody Herman in his small band, and we went to Washington D.C., and some cat... Boy, I don't know, some cat was dancing with this girl and he stuck his…

170.t: Switching to drums and the curiosity about drugs
170.s: Ware loses his basses and gets curious about dope; with Gloria he discusses drugs in the black community.
170.ch: Drugs and the House of Correction
170.q: Well, that's an area, too, that should be talked about. A lot of people try to dismiss that -- we were reading a story called 'Will the Circle Be Unbroken?' and it was, in a sense, it showed that that is a part of the black community, even though the black community doesn't manufacture it or import…

170.t: Brooklyn, drinking, A.A. and the Amherst workshop
170.s: Ware drinks heavily; Gloria suggests A.A., and he plays workshops and a college date with Billy Higgins.
170.ch: Monk, Ellington and Archie Shepp in the 1970s
170.q: Then I moved up to Brooklyn, moved out to the house that Billy Higgins, drummer, was living in. Gloria and I took a ground-floor apartment and moved the furniture from Philly over there -- piano and everything. But by then, I was drinking this vodka like it was going out of style and Gloria started…

170.t: Nodding on the bandstand and losing the fiddles
170.s: Ware snorts heroin, nods off on stage, and loses his two basses.
170.ch: Drugs and the House of Correction
170.q: And I'm working every night, right in the midst of it, and the guys would come back and say, "Hey, take a little snort of this" -- he said, "You won't get a habit" -- so I snorted it, and went back up on the bandstand, and the drummer was the leader of the band -- a little cat named Bill Pinkert,…

170.t: The Calumet City strip joints and Jive Jackson
170.s: Ware plays drums for strip acts in Calumet City in a band whose leader supplied pills to keep his habit going.
170.ch: Drugs and the House of Correction
170.q: The strip joints . See, everybody at one time worked out there. Vernell was working down the street, Ike had in fact, he showed me how to play one lady's act -- a lady called Tanalia -- she worked with snakes -- a mystic type thing, alligator -- we had 5 pieces out there. And the guy that had the…

170.t: His first whiskey in Quincy as a teenager
170.s: He drinks a pitcher of whiskey at fifteen in Quincy and is violently sick.
170.ch: Drugs and the House of Correction
170.q: Same thing. When I first went to Quincy, Illinois, with the band -- not Flip's band, but this other band, Roy, I hadn't -- I mean, I would drink a little wine with the gang, because there were 10 of us on one pint, you know, and we'd swear we were high. But when I got to Quincy, they were serving…

171.t: Drinking on the job and a drummer's habits
171.s: The band rarely drank on the job; Ramey tells about a drummer drunk afternoons and nights and his marriage.
171.ch: Meeting Jay McShann and Martin's on the Plaza
171.q: We very seldom would drink on the job, you know. I think when we finally got Bird, he may have goofed a little hit. But everybody pretty much was a gentleman, and took care of the job pretty good.

171.t: Drinkers against dope users and the 52nd Street arrests
171.s: Drug users condemned drinkers as drunks; Ramey and Sid Catlett recall the roundup of twenty-four on 52nd Street.
171.ch: New York: 52nd Street and Lester Young
171.q: Definitely, yeah. Well, I tell you another thing that happened in there at the time. First of all, remember that the guys who -- who drank whiskey could be condemned by the guys who were on the other side of the Street, who used dope, you know. And they'd come over and see you

171.t: Heroin and the straight sound; Ben Webster's rhythm section
171.s: Heroin-era players abandoned growls and effects; Ben Webster dropped his buzz, and his rhythm section was one of 52nd Street's best.
171.ch: New York: 52nd Street and Lester Young
171.q: No, let me -- advance, what you're saying, the way I see it from just what you said there, when those heroin smokers started coming out on the street, that ended the career for lots of trumpet players who could have played, like Cootie Williams, could have done a thing like Tricky Sam, you know.…

171.t: Becoming close friends with McShann, who drank
171.s: Ramey kept the job and they became close friends while McShann was drinking heavily.
171.ch: Meeting Jay McShann and Martin's on the Plaza
171.q: Well, became very close friends. In fact, Hadnott was available to John right then, but he didn't want to join John until Gus came. And so I went in for the two weeks. But evidently -- anyway, the two weeks was up and Hadnott they had

171.s: Bird stayed in control while followers copied him; he introduced nutmeg and soaked reeds in benzedrine water. Ramey never took drugs.
171.ch: Bird, the band's breakup and Luis Russell
171.q: Well, it wasn't that same way it was doing to Jackknife, scratching his chin, you know, scratching his face, which is always an obvious sign, you know. It wasn't that. In fact, it's very rarely you would see him doing the way, he was standing there nodding and that sort of thing.

241.t: Thomas in brass bands and leaving the drinking players
241.s: Thomas names the brass bands he played in and tells why he stopped working with them after a player joined church.
241.q: I was a regular member in John's band. Yeah. Yeah, I just got out after them fellas man, that fellas that like the auger too much, you know what I mean? Had a fella that he like the auger, man and Gabbert, he said, I like the auger so much, you know. So, I got this guy, me and this boy Albert, you…

241.t: Clarinetists Lili and Edmond Hall; levee dances and not drinking
241.s: He recalls the clarinetist Lili, who quit playing, and says Edmond Hall had a gift and rose quickly. The same block continues with playing dances on the porch and levee and his never being a drinker.
241.q: I was playing with that band. After all these boys left from there, I went to play with that band. You know what I mean? Oh yeah, you're talking about, uh, well he got a French name. Lili. That's his name. That's all I know his name, Lili. He was a good boy, you know that boy was a nice, class day.…

241.t: Not drinking; tea and coffee on the Japan trip
241.s: He says he never drank much and quit coffee, and recalls sleeplessness from tea and coffee in Japan.
241.q: I just don't care about it. I have liquor at home then, what you call, gave me a bottle of champagne, man. A really genuine champagne. Gave me that for going with praise when I was going in there. And you know I still got that bottle of champagne in there. Tell somebody to come in and drink it. I'm…

241.t: Drinking banter and his wife Babe
241.s: The interviewer teases about whiskey; Valentine says he only drinks a little beer, and they talk about his wife's nickname.
241.q: So, uh, uh, okay. You want to get it? Yeah, yeah, yeah. What do you call your wife? Call a babe.

303.t: Drinking on the bandstand and Monk Hazel
303.s: Nobody drank on the stand with Sharkey's band, and Sharkey never drank; Monk Hazel came to work drunk but always repaid loans.
303.q: No. During the missions, we all did, with the exception of Sharky. Maybe he had a beer once in a while, but Sharky never did drink. I never did see Sharky drink a high ball in my life.

303.s: Riddick says smoking was never done on the stand with Sharkey at the Famous Door or the Blue Room; he himself quit 22 years ago.
303.q: Some places, yes. Some places, no. Naturally, I have no way of commenting on it anymore because I just don't smoke. I haven't smoked in 22 years. Really? I haven't touched one of any kind. My goodness.

303.t: Smoking marijuana in the 1920s, bought on St. Philip Street
303.s: Recalls how marijuana was bought through a hole in a wall, then then-illegal status and price.
303.ch: Gulf Coast bands and early jobs
303.q: If you want to get it, if you want to talk a little bit about smoking grass, those days was, it's so different than it is today that it's pitiful. It was a sin to smoke grass when I smoked grass.

303.t: Prohibition-era drinking on the road and now
303.s: Riddick describes quarts of white lightning at dances and says he seldom drinks now.
303.q: Very much so until you got to where you were playing. And when you started to play that night, as a general rule, the guy that ran the dance brought you a quart of whiskey. And it would knock your head off. Sometimes 110 proof alcohol. Call it white lightning or mountain dew. It's all according to…

1.t: Wilbur De Paris takes the tips and bans drinking
1.s: In Wilbur De Paris's band Wilbur kept the tips for promotion and told players off for drinking.
1.ch: Danny's rise through New York bands to Cab Calloway
1.q: have no money. He was the first musician that I know who said the tips belonged to him. See, the people would come to the bandstand and say, "Ten dollars, play a 'Saints' or play so-and-so." And he'd put his (?) and say, "We've got some tips." So I'd say, "Well, where is the tips money, man?" He…

1.t: Bill Douglas's drunken drive and apology through Lu
1.s: After a drive through the Bronx, Danny told Bill never to call again, but Bill phoned Lu repeatedly to apologize.
1.ch: Arriving in New York: the Nest Club and Harlem nightlife
1.q: I was doing "St. James Infirmary," and Bill was playing nothing. I could get high with Bill, see. See, he gave us all the whiskey we'd want. One time I said, "Brother, I'm finished. I'm tired. I don't want to work with you any more. You get you somebody else." No, he would tell me, when we were…

1.s: Smitty has coffee, and Danny and Milt recall how whiskey kept them going and that poor diet shortened lives like King Oliver's.
1.ch: Chicago, Lee Collins and the road
1.q: Or we would have had a bottle. But when you get up to a certain age, you have to watch your diet. That diet business, huh? If they had had a diet in the early Thirties, King Oliver and all of them people probably would have been living. But they didn't have the proper diet.

1.t: The trio at Morton's Cafeteria and Lu's beer
1.s: Lu and Danny worked a trio with Louis Metcalf at a cafeteria on 57th Street, where Lu, then 218 pounds, defied Danny's no-beer rule.
1.ch: Lu Barker and the Barbarin family
1.q: Danny used to tell me... I used to like to drink beer. "See, singers, these people they don't be drinkin' no beer, because you'll be belching all over the people." Now, I weighed 218 pounds.

147.t: Never on dope; drug use among musicians
147.s: Crawford says no one in his band used drugs and describes seeing an overdose in the hospital.
147.ch: The Lunceford years: Europe, rivals and bandsmen
147.q: Perhaps so, but nobody in my band, in our band. I never was on dope. I don't see how a man can function himself and sniff cocaine and all that stuff. It was very expensive. I never in my life even saw anybody do it. Never. Oh, yes, I did.

147.t: Crawford and Al Norris as the band's drinkers
147.s: Crawford says he was the ringleader who drank with Al Norris and Willie Smith, while Wilcox drank little.
147.q: Al Norris and myself and Willie Woody Smith, they all died last (inaudible). Al Norris and I, we'd drink anything we could get our hands on. Willie Woody Smith also. He died, unfortunately. He was a great saxophone player. Wilcox didn't do too much of drinking, but that Al Norris and myself, we…

147.t: Lunceford's manners and his brother Connie
147.s: Crouch probes Lunceford's discipline and Crawford talks about his family and his valet brother Connie, a heavy drinker.
147.q: Yeah, very nice people, out of Warren, Ohio. He had a brother that could drink as much whiskey as Al Norris and I, by the name of Connie Lunsford. He was a valet. Yes, he really could -- I mean he drank -- he drank pretty heavy. Lunsford used to look at him in disgust. He never would say anything…

147.t: Willie Smith's constant reading and his cigarette ritual
147.s: Crawford describes Willie Smith always reading and saying a prayer before handing over a cigarette.
147.ch: Road life, segregation and band pranks
147.q: Always, always reading. He was a peculiar person. He was from Charleston, South Carolina, so he'd be sitting there, reading, smoking a cigarette, always had a book in front of him, always, when he was walking the streets, always was reading. He had a bottle of whisky. And so -- didn't read much. I…

384.t: Goldkette lets the band go; musicians too drunk to find their chairs
384.s: Goldkette handled bookings and let the band do as it liked; Morehouse recalls players feeling for their chairs yet playing like mad.
384.ch: Bix, Trumbauer and the Goldkette sidemen
384.q: So he took care of I guess the booking and whatever was there. Because my brother Charlie was right in there trying to make the fellows play, and behave

384.t: Bix's drinking and the band's drinking and spitballs
384.s: They discuss how Bix's drinking affected his playing, and how the whole band drank and acted like kids, driving Virginia's father to leave.
384.ch: Bix, Trumbauer and the Goldkette sidemen
384.q: When they began on the stand to rehearse, they would cut up and they would throw spitballs.

384.t: Doc Ryker takes charge of the unruly band
384.s: Charlie Horvath turned discipline over to Doc Ryker, a teetotaler and former scoutmaster, who treated the band like Boy Scouts.
384.ch: Bix, Trumbauer and the Goldkette sidemen
384.q: Well he used to do a lot of swearing. And that's when Doc Ryker stepped in. Now Doc was a very...He was the only one I would say who was the most

384.t: Paul Mertz, Jimmy Dorsey and the musicians' reputations
384.s: Mertz was a great pianist who did not drink, Jimmy Dorsey was a drinker, and the group are remembered as gentlemen.
384.ch: Bix, Trumbauer and the Goldkette sidemen
384.q: Yeah. Well if you see them tonight, if you would run into one, he would treat you like a gentleman.

412.t: Drummer Earl Wiley, Dave Tough and four trumpets at the Liberty Inn
412.s: Hodes tells how the bosses tracked Earl Wiley's drinking and pawned drums, and how Dave Tough sat in. He recalls four trumpets on one stand, with Pee Wee dropping in, and cheap gin.
412.q: But until he made that speech, everything was great. They tolerated him. But with that speech, it's funny how that -- everything turned around and he was walking frontwards and all that, just with Johnny shaking him. I got the story from Earl Wiley. I wasn't there at the time. Tut was working…

412.t: Drummer Earl Wiley, Dave Tough and four trumpets at the Liberty Inn
412.s: Hodes tells how the bosses tracked Earl Wiley's drinking and pawned drums, and how Dave Tough sat in. He recalls four trumpets on one stand, with Pee Wee dropping in, and cheap gin.

But with that speech, it's funny how that -- everything turned around and he was walking frontwards and all that, just with Johnny shaking him. I got the story from Earl Wiley. I wasn't there at the time. Tut was working…

412.t: The Pirate's Den and the George Zack stories
412.s: Hodes plays solo at the Pirate's Den. He tells stories about pianist George Zack's drinking, from the hotel room that never opened to the Lyons, Illinois job that George Hoefer found.
412.ch: Back Room, Solo Art and George Zack (corrected typing)
412.q: So eventually, I got a crack at something else. I worked in the Village at the Pirate's Den, as a solo. And about then, Zack came to New York, George Zack. And the boss at the Pirate's Den was very fascinated with him. And he just dreamt about having the two of us. But if you know something about…

412.t: The Pirate's Den and the George Zack stories
412.s: Hodes plays solo at the Pirate's Den. He tells stories about pianist George Zack's drinking, from the hotel room that never opened to the Lyons, Illinois job that George Hoefer found.
412.ch: Back Room, Solo Art and George Zack (retyped)
412.q: So eventually, I got a crack at something else. I worked in the Village at the Pirate's Den, as a solo. And about then, Zack came to New York, George Zack. And the boss at the Pirate's Den was very fascinated with him. And he just dreamt about having the two of us. But if you know something about…

30.t: Sonny Greer's drinking and the Kansas City druggist's fake drink
30.s: Duke had a Kansas City druggist serve Sonny a fake drink, which made Sonny pass out anyway; Bigard adds that Sonny had a phenomenal memory for names.
30.ch: Ellington band: drinking, quarrels and rent parties
30.q: Yeah, we were in Kansas City and Sonny used to get stoned every night so much and Duke was getting after him. Duke was getting after him to stop drinking so much because it was interfering with his music. So they had a drug store in Kansas City that this druggist was taking alcohol and doctoring it…

30.t: How Ben Webster got Bigard drinking and telling Duke off
30.s: He did not drink until he saw Ben Webster curse Duke without answer, so he began on sherry with Johnny Hodges's wife and told Duke off all the time.
30.ch: Ellington band: drinking, quarrels and rent parties
30.q: When I joined the band I didn't drink at all, and what started me drinking was Ben Webster. You see, like Duke sometimes would scold me for something, an insignificant thing. Ben Webster used to come in the band to get stoned and raise holy hell and cuss him out and everything else. Duke don't say…

30.s: Otto Hardwick often missed nights; when Bigard went along, Hardwick ran from apartment to apartment drinking until Bigard missed the job.
30.q: You see, I was -- that was after I joined Duke. And during the summer I used to go up in the New England states when he had the big band, see, and that's when he used to tell all the stories about Sidney and Bubber Miley and Otto Hardwick -- that's another one.

30.t: Whether Duke drank, and the rent parties
30.s: Duke was not a heavy drinker in Bigard's time; the rent parties, or chitlin switches, served the world's worst bathtub gin.
30.ch: Ellington band: drinking, quarrels and rent parties
30.q: Well, you see, those guys used to play those -- they called them "chitlin switches" and that's their rent parties, you know, house rent parties. That's so they can get enough money to pay the rent, and they used to have all kind of -- bathtub gin and all, the world's worst.

112.t: Opium, cocaine and the sporting life in Newark
112.s: He says there was no marijuana then, only hop and cocaine, and describes pimps with opium pipes who tried to break him in.
112.q: Johnny Vikal. He had a big act on that and he did very well with that. And what he used was, 'Chinatown' for his music, you know, and he did a dope fiend act.

112.t: Taking Charley Johnson's Newark job; first dope fiend
112.s: Charley Johnson recommends Wooding for his Newark job and shows him a drug user nodding off at the piano.
112.q: And, but the funny thing, the first time I'd ever seen a dope fiend, too. I didn't know nothing about the dope fiends or nothing like that.

112.t: Atlantic City's Paradise ownership and Prohibition drinking
112.s: He says Charley Johnson worked the Boardwalk while the Paradise changed hands, and that Prohibition increased drinking and bad liquor.
112.ch: Philadelphia, Detroit and back to Atlantic City
112.q: Well, at that time, let's see. No, Charley was working on the Boardwalk. And the man had the -- Al Branch had a place there where the Paradise was. But Ralph (Wheelock) hadn't taken it over. He took it over that summer, or the end of that summer. Cause Charley lived the year round at Atlantic City…

112.t: Rent party prices, bootleg drink and learning to drink
112.s: Albertson asks about the parties; Wooding gives prices, mentions blackberry and gin, and a friend's mother warning them apart.
112.q: : I was very seldom in Atlantic City in the wintertime, because we was only down there with my father. See, and he worked and when Labor Day, then we all came home.

259.t: Kid Shots, cornetist who deputised for Little Joe
259.s: Vincent calls Kid Shots a good cornet player who liked whiskey and filled in for Little Joe for two weeks. He says dance-hall rules about children hurt their work.
259.ch: Casa, Zeb Lenard and Little Joe
259.q: How about kid shots? Oh, you remember kid shots? Oh, good. Yeah. Yeah. He was another good corner player. Uh... I look ahead of him up, too. Ooh, that man can drink some whiskey. Yeah, I mean... Well, kid shots was good.

259.t: Teaching Little Joe the trumpet, and his later troubles
259.s: Vincent taught the 14-year-old Little Joe to play horn by picking his banjo, within four months Joe could blow. He tells of Joe's marijuana and whiskey habits, his later breakdown and turn to preaching, and chats about where they live.
259.ch: Casa, Zeb Lenard and Little Joe
259.q: He sure was at that time. Yeah, he must have been along the other day. 32 when I met him, because I took his place with Nat Toll, what he talking about.

259.t: Tony Jackson, the solo pianist, and drummer Bruno Joseph
259.s: Vincent remembers Tony Jackson as a well-known solo piano player who did not play with bands. He then describes drummer Bruno Joseph, who died after drinking bad corn whiskey.
259.ch: Banjo career, Armstrong and the Liberty Bell
259.q: So he wanted to tell us about Tony Jackson. Tony Jackson? Well, Tony Jackson, that fellow was a, you know, this cabinet player. He used to play on hold, you know, all the time. He was a piano player. He used to say he was a morphedizer, you know. And the other part of it too, Bunnell. Both of them…

251.s: Albert says he never acted like the underworld characters around him, and the pair agree vice is overstated.
251.ch: Parades, vice and the New Orleans scene
251.q: Well, I have never been a shitty character. Let's don't believe that I fell in the footsteps of those guys, because I never have. But they never acted like shitty characters around me. There was always a friendly gesture.

251.t: Refined, well-behaved men in Albert's band
251.s: Compared with Lunsford's college men, Albert's band members were gentlemen, many schooled with Cottrell, and almost none drank.
251.q: Not too well, just a few of them. I remember when the singer Al Hibbler went to Jay McShann. He was probably, all of the guys in there knew me personally. Mm-hmm. But, I've forgotten quite a number of those guys unless they come up and refresh my memory and then I can recognize them.

251.s: Allen asks about Floyd Snelson, and Albert calls him his publicity man, a great newspaper writer with a drinking problem.
251.q: Sure, Floyd was my publicity man. He was a great, great newspaper man, but he had a problem. Alcohol. But he was one of the greatest writers that you ever want to see. And on one of my band pictures you see Floyd Snellson leaning out of the window.

23.s: Reefers were legal and common in New Orleans until 1936; Rose doubts he picked it up as a kid.
23.q: I'm sure, because, you know, in New Orleans, uh, uh, first place, the Harrison Act didn't come into effect until 1936. Right. So, it wasn't illegal.

23.t: Opium and cocaine in early New Orleans
23.s: Opium was around, cocaine legal; Eugene Dasty put it on sale in his drugstore window.
23.q: Well, in his neighborhood, what was hot was opium. Yeah. And people used to run opium. Mm-hmm. But, uh, you know, opium was an elaborate thing to go through, you had to have all the equipment and everything, and most people didn't bother with that. In fact, there wasn't a big thing with drugs in…

23.s: Armstrong pushed his laxative on everyone, though Rose says it was not a New Orleans product.
23.q: I have no knowledge of it. Okay. I know that he bothered everybody with it. Yeah, right. Passed out packets of it.

450.t: The mental hospital, shock treatment and detox attempts in London and Scotland
450.s: The supposed rehab turns out to be a locked psychiatric ward; she relapses, tries a London detox clinic and a rented house in Scotland while still using.
450.q: No. It’s another name. I’ll try to think of it. Of course I got out of it before I went there. I noticed a girl checking in with her parents, and I thought, you have to sign in? All right. Then a member of the staff came, a woman, huge. We went up to a floor. We got out. The first sign I got of…

450.t: Her brother's ultimatum, Majorca and quitting cold turkey
450.s: A doctor warns she will never stop and her brother withdraws help; after Majorca she returns, quits cold turkey, starts working alone and speaks of Dave Lambert as the group's founder.
450.q: been in a prisoner of war camp. She won’t make it. She’s not ever going to stop. You’ve got to face it,” blah blah. My brother – I remember it was raining. We went outside. He said, “Annie, I have my own life. I can’t do it anymore. You’re going to have to do it on your own.” I said, “All I really…

450.t: Willard Alexander, touring with Basie and her heroin habit
450.s: She is persuaded to return, plays with Basie in the US and Europe, but her drug use escalates and Jon and Dave arrange a hospital stay.
450.q: I’m trying to think of outstanding things. Oh, after we had done Basie, I left for Europe. I went to France on holiday. I kept getting letters from Jon and Dave. “Come back. We can do an act.” I thought, they’re nuts. How can three people get up, except with smoke and mirrors, and get up? How are…

471.t: Republic Gardens with Charlie Rouse and Cedric Williams
471.s: Rouse formed a band at Republic Gardens on U Street; Cobb describes the players and seeing a pianist's drug use.
471.ch: Growing up and learning drums in Washington
471.q: I don’t want to put – it’s just like kissing and tell. I ain’t going to do that. There’s a lot of things that happened that a whole lot of people really don’t need to know about. So I’m going to keep it like that. That’s where I draw the line. Mentioning about being up on the main drag, U Street,…

471.s: Brower and Cobb discuss Lexington, where players checked themselves in to clean out.
471.ch: Bird, Coltrane and Dinah Washington recollections
471.q: Oh yeah. All them guys went through it. I think they thought it was cleansing their bodies so they could get higher quicker or something like that. I don’t know what they did. They have a vacation or something there.

471.s: Cobb discusses Jimmy Heath, who went to Lexington, and praises his autobiography.
471.ch: Bird, Coltrane and Dinah Washington recollections
471.q: Yeah. Well, Jimmy Heath was – Jimmy Heath went to the – at one time they was calling Jimmy Heath “Little Bird.” I guess Jimmy just got to tenor. He was playing tenor. He was – Jimmy was a bandleader way back there. Before Percy started to play the bass, Jimmy was a bandleader. Percy used to carry…

228.s: In 1946-47 drugs arrived in Harlem and his idols used them; left alone, he tried heroin at a dance and gradually increased use.
228.ch: Heroin and the Miles Davis years
228.q: That in itself was kind of like a phenomenon. I came up in Harlem. I never knew of any drugs or anything like that the whole time I was coming up, until the end of World War II. It seemed like from the minute World War II was over, 1946, ’47, that it began to make its appearance in my neighborhood…

228.s: After six months in jail, served four and a half, and help from a doctor who held him together with Dollie, he stopped; he was tired of jail.
228.ch: Later Blue Note years and ending the habit
228.q: I went to jail and stayed in jail for a six-month period. I got out in four months and 15 days on good behavior. Came home. Then I had a doctor that had been writing me letters and that wanted to see me. I went to see her. She was very helpful in getting me – keeping me together, holding me…

228.t: No social circle around the Blue Note dates
228.s: The musicians were his choice but not friends; he and Walter Davis ran together while Donald Byrd and Paul Chambers were clean.
228.ch: Blue Note, The Connection and Tony Williams
228.q: Well, there was a musical circle. Remember I said I didn’t – not on a sociable level. I didn’t have a circle of guys that I kind of hung out with after the date and we went over to a bar and sat down and talked or nothing. I didn’t have time for that, and neither did anybody else there hardly.…

114.t: Drinking too much and not knowing music
114.s: Moody says he drank heavily because people praised him though he knew no music and did not know he should practice.
114.ch: Alcohol, Paris and the hit record
114.q: -- but I mean, I just drank too much. And I know why I was drinking, now. The reason -- one of the reasons I was drinking was because -- well, first of all -- and -- and it lingered on till when I had my septet. And the reason was because people say, "Boy, you sound good." But I didn't know any…

114.t: Sake night in Tokyo and staying away from stimulants
114.s: He recalls a drunken night with Dizzy and Oliver Nelson in Japan, and says he avoids alcohol and drugs.
114.q: Oh yeah. Yeah. But it was -- Oh, we had a hell of a night in, in Tokyo because me, Michael Lungo, him, and Oliver Nelson (phonetic sp.) all was lit with the sake. And then he says, for the people, you know, for all the people in Japan, he says "I know what I'm gonna do." He says, "I'm gonna tell…

114.s: He admitted himself to Overbrook for six months, realizing he drank because he was praised yet felt he knew nothing.
114.q: Yeah. Yeah. Uh-huh (affirmative). I drank. I went to Overbrook because I drank too much alcohol. And I stayed at that thing maybe six months. Something like that.

373.t: Heroin and the jazz subculture: Bird, Miles and Bud Powell
373.s: Hentoff recalls the Parker-inspired drug culture, Miles Davis quitting cold turkey, and Bud Powell asking him for money.
373.q: There was a period, and this is well known, when – and I think Bird had something to do with it – people felt – it was like a religious thing – he played so brilliantly, so originally, and he was on heroin, so maybe if I got on stuff . . . . I don’t there was necessarily a direct tie with…

373.t: Was heroin put in the black community on purpose?
373.s: He dismisses the conspiracy theory as unsubstantiated and ties it to government surveillance conspiracies today.
373.q: Oh yeah. There were all kinds of horrible things that totally defaced the Constitution that J. Edgar Hoover and other people did, but this kind of conspiracy theory – there was never anything to substantiate it. People tried very hard. But this goes on all the time. This is how now, with the kind…

373.t: Why Ben Webster, Coleman Hawkins and Lester Young drank
373.s: He discusses each man's drinking and temperament and doubts that race alone explains their sad ends.
373.q: They didn’t all wind up like that in some kind of terminal way. It was a process up and down. I never thought of Coleman Hawkins – although I knew that he drank and all that – whenever I’d seen him, he was still the magisterial Coleman Hawkins. Ben – and this was well known to musicians – when he…

66.t: Bel Canto Foundation: helping musicians off heroin with prayers and music
66.s: She helped addict musicians by keeping them with her and having them play drum parts she wrote.
66.ch: Church, Bel Canto and the return to music
66.q: : I decided that I wanted to help the few - well, after comparing rock I said the few - few musicians that were using dope, jazz musicians that were using dope. I decided I'd like to help them and so I went on out on my own with a method of my own. I had success with two.

66.t: What the Bel Canto Foundation was
66.s: A foundation to help addicts and alcoholics; her lawyer thought the board strange.
66.ch: Church, Bel Canto and the return to music
66.q: : Now that is something else. My lawyer said to me, "This is the strangest board I've ever seen. The president never has a board meeting or I don't know what she's doing. I think we all better leave her alone before we go to jail." The lawyer, Bill (Sousa(?)), terrific. Father Woods called him. He…

66.t: Taking Monk and Bud to church
66.s: Monk, Hal Baker and Bud Powell met her at Our Lady of Lourdes; Monk drank wine first and fell in the door.
66.ch: Church, Bel Canto and the return to music
66.q: : Not immediately. I used to give prayers for musicians and Monk, Hal Baker, Bud Powell in the summer would meet me at the Lady of Lourdes. Mass went on at 6:30 then, I think, or 7. They'd meet me at 6 o'clock and they'd go in church with me. I'd keep them through three masses. The first time I…

409.t: Starting to drink after forming his own band
409.s: Cootie began drinking some two years after forming his band, drinking and then laying off, and quit entirely in the late 1950s.
409.q: I don't know. Maybe handling men and seeing their reaction and going out on parties, with people inviting you out, and the thing that I never did drink. So I started to drinking.

409.t: Sonny Greer's drinking and why Cootie wanted to leave
409.s: Cootie got angry at Sonny's drinking and falling off the drums, one reason he wanted to leave.
409.q: Yeah. That was the main reason why. That was one of the main reasons why I wanted to leave, too. Because he didn't care. He'd get drunk and fall off the drums and things like that. And it wasn't no good for me.

409.t: The voyage to England, poker and not drinking
409.s: On the crossing the band played poker all night while Duke drank brandy and champagne; Cootie did not drink until he had his band.
409.q: Yeah. He'd sit up, and he'd be drinking brandy and champagne. In those days I wasn't drinking.

231.t: Drinking to spite Nazarro, and his later two sets of books
231.s: Bubbles got drunk on set to undercut Nazarro, who kept the studio going all night; Nazarro later died with two sets of books.
231.q: That's right. But he really, not like him to get that way -- let him -- God rest his soul. However, getting back where I was trying to explain to you concerning the two checks. That showed me he was stealing. I didn't know that. Instead of me discarding him from that point on I went on like nothing…

231.t: Buck and marijuana: the police raid in Toronto
231.s: Buck had taken up marijuana with musician friends; at his Toronto hotel the police arrived while Bubbles was visiting to learn a song.
231.q: However, I passed that stage and I come on into another movement of where I've got to get out of New York again. I didn't like it. They didn't want to pay the salary, that was it. They didn't want to pay the salary.

231.t: Winning the case, and marijuana found later in his car
231.s: Bubbles beat his case with AGVA's help, then discovered Buck had hidden marijuana in his glove compartment.
231.q: that's what it was. They got me for being with them and my reason for being with them and I got the AGVA to stand for me in the trial they had and everything. I won my case. But later on I found out this guy had stashed stuff in the car. Buck had stashed stuff in my car and I didn't know it and…

0.s: Swindell, who lived next door to Charlie Parker, might have rivalled Parker had drugs not ruined him; he died after moving to the West Coast.
0.ch: The Jelly Roll Morton records and Minton's Playhouse
0.q: Yeah. Yeah, we had a boy there -- his wife is living in New York now. She was a very good musician. Name's Swindell, an alto player. If he hadn't of died, if he hadn't got on that stuff, I think he'd have been close to Charlie Parker. He used to come down there all the time. I'd say, go on,…

0.t: Hawkins's decline: vodka, the beard and rumours
0.s: Caldwell heard Hawkins was drinking two fifths a day and not eating; Charlie Holmes described him as an old man of the mountains.
0.ch: Benny Carter, saxophones and Coleman Hawkins's last years
0.q: [Baptist] funeral parlor. His daughter was working there at the same time, when he passed. But we were down there at the River Boat. That's when they gave this thing for Red Allen, and Louie Metcalf was in charge of it. So I went down with Jimmy Rushing, couple of us together, and so the girl came…

0.t: Chu Berry's portrait at the Elks Home in Charleston, West Virginia
0.s: On tour with Tiny Bradshaw, Caldwell found Chu's picture at the Elks home, where knowing Chu meant free drinks.
0.q: Uh-huh. So we said, well, we got a day off. Let's go down to the Elks' Home. So I said, okay, let's go to the Elks' Home, you know, you don't go there to buy ain't nothing just to go around have a ball. So we got down there and up against the wall behind the bar was Chu Berry's picture. So I told…

71.s: Musicians had nowhere to go after two a.m. but whiskey places, which Clayton and Dance link to alcoholism.
71.q: Right, that's right. Only thing is that after you get through at two o'clock in the morning there's nothing but whiskey places that you can go. You can't go anywhere else that doesn't sell whiskey at two o'clock in the morning.

71.t: Shaky nerves for weeks after slivovitch and rum

265.t: Dope addiction on the old corner
265.s: Addiction was less common then; he saw addicts start at his corner for 21 years.

And I saw 95% of the dope addicts around here start off right on that corner. I know boys from a good family, swell boys. And I, you see, they had them big old doves.…

265.s: Sam Morgan played soft at Economy Hall while Rena played loud and drank; Punch Miller is recovering, and musicians bum all night.

215.t: Why musicians got into drugs and trouble

976.t: Studying Buddhism with Trungpa at Naropa

134.t: When drugs came into the music scene

451.t: Upsides and downsides of nightclub life

108.t: Why jazz was held in contempt

372.s: The story of Gerry Mulligan passing him a pipe at a theater rehearsal and a solo he nearly missed.

27.t: First night under King Oliver's name: the band gets drunk in Hayes, Kansas
27.s: At their first dance under King Oliver's name, several players got drunk on homemade drink, and Oliver nearly dismissed them; Phillips and others scolded them.
27.q: : Well, let me tell you this about King Oliver. The first night that we played with King Oliver, when King Oliver took the band over, we went to a little old town called... I think it was Hayes, Kansas.

68.t: The Hotel Lincoln bar tunnel and Byas's drinking

68.ch: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band

146.t: Sleeping, eating, drinking and gambling on the road
146.s: The band slept in beds four or five nights a week, ate cold cuts, barely drank, knew no marijuana until about 1939, and only two gambled.
146.ch: Road life, arranging and racial dangers
146.q: No, we'd stop on the road in little groceries, drive-ins and things, pick up little sandwiches and whatnot, little cold-cuts. What the boys called cold-cuts -- sardines and stuff like that. Black ham.

70.t: Saxophonists Bill Graham and Rick Henderson
70.s: Bill Graham got everyone drinking Thunderbird wine and was let go; Rick Henderson, a bebop-influenced alto from Washington, joined and Procope took more lead.
70.ch: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
70.q: Then Bill Graham. He was in there for a while. But Bill Graham, he had everybody drinking his wine, so Duke thought he'd better get rid of him.

452.t: Cliques in Hampton's band and his drinking buddies
452.s: Hampton's band was a syndicate of groups; Cobb fell in with Milton Buckner, Jack McVea, Fred Beckett and Al Hayes, who were drinkers rather than users.
452.q: No, it wasn't the same thing because that was too much of a syndicated situation in that band, different groups for different things. 232.t: Firing Artis Paul in Las Vegas and the union hearing
232.s: Fields pays off drunk Artis Paul rather than use him in Las Vegas; Artis files charges and then confirms Fields' account.

383.t: Big Green's drinking system in Benny Carter's band
383.s: Wilson tells how trombonist Big Green drank on a system and would lend money but never share his whisky.
383.q: Yeah, I worked with Big Green a long time in Benny Carter's band. Yeah, he was a great sax and trombone player. Always hit those long notes for us, he was powerful.

94.t: The drug scene among Los Angeles musicians
94.s: Moore says drug use was around but not yet a big problem, and he used it only to be part of the crowd.
94.q: All around town, but it wasn't quite a big problem yet as it is now. We knew who was using it and I don't know where the supply comes from, but I tried it for a while just to be in with the crowd but it never -- I never got used to it, so I left it alone a few more years and it wasn't too much of a…

235.t: Drugs around the musicians and why he stayed away
235.s: Friends used heroin to concentrate on music; he understood but declined, and helped when he could.
235.ch: The Paradise and life in Queens
235.q: Well, I'll tell you something. I never ... I won't mention any names ... they tried to romance me into this, but I just didn't... 95.t: Victoria Spivey and Bessie Smith: cussing and drinking
95.s: She says Spivey was a mean woman who cussed and drank, and contrasts Bessie Smith's way of taking over a party.
95.q: She said, 'I like the way you sing my 'Black Snake.'" (Unintelligible), but she say, 'I like the way you sing my 'Black Snake,' because you sing it better than I did.'"

454.t: Fear of Parker, Dizzy, Bud and Max; drugs and manners
454.s: Mingus was wary of the bebop circle's drugs and cursing and only came to love Bird later.
454.ch: Massey Hall, race and the record business
454.q: I was afraid of those guys, because they you know, they were so famous: all used drugs. (Inaudible) Max was a junkie, Bird was a junkie, Bud Powell was a junkie, and Dizzy was crazy. 96.t: 'Muggles' and tea in the jazz world
96.s: He explains the terms muggle and tea, Mezzrow, and his own limited use.
96.q: Oh yes. Well anyone who has read about Milton Mezzrow, he was a guy hanging around. He didn't play too well. 168.q: Yes. Well, I didn't dwell on that too much, about the different fellows. Of course, when you speak of dissipation and what have you, I imagine we all had our little things going for us that weren't too kosher. 611.t: Giving up drinking in 1969 and smoking in 1935
611.s: Waters quit drinking in 1969 after losing his appetite and quit smoking around 1935, leaving overwork as his only vice.
611.q: Well, I gave up drinkin' on account of I couldn't eat, I [was] just losing appetite and going without food for two or three days all in New York, you know -

388.t: Giving up drinking after seven years of sobriety
388.s: Leeman, who started drinking at 14, quit cold turkey about seven years earlier because it was killing him, helped by his wife, Ralph Sutton and Dick Gibson, and learned he could play without it.
388.q: Well, I used to carry my chef's outfit around -- but that was really in the great days during my really drinking days. Of course, I started drinking when I was 14 years old.

74.t: Bobby Moore, a holdup, and Bobby Carroll joins
74.s: A holdup at a club, Moore's suicide, and Bobby Carroll joins and stays about ten years.
74.ch: Leading his own band in New York
74.q: He was getting a little flighty because we had a place--one night the place was held up and I noticed everybody was walking towards the back with their hands in the air, I didn't know what it was all about, and Bobby stood up with his trumpet, then I saw all these guns. 237.t: The night before Moten's tonsillectomy with Dr. Bruce
237.s: Lovett recalls Moten and Dr. Bruce drinking and playing pool on 18th Street the night before the operation.
237.ch: Bennie Moten, Basie and the Reno
237.q: Pretty good. He'd beat me, that's one thing and so he was a wonderful man, wonderful man and that night I was on 18th Street when he and Dr. Bruce, they were running together, you know.

124.t: The clean life of band musicians
124.s: The pay was modest but the life was clean; players in top bands had to live like gentlemen, with little drug use.
124.ch: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
124.q: To get in a band like Fletcher Henderson or Chick Webb or -- Teddy Hill had a good band -- or another band -- young guy with a great band, you know -- from the time that Teddy Wilson had his band.

76.t: Zutty the gentleman: finer things, horse shows
76.s: Marge says musicians are wrongly pictured as drunkards; Zutty was neat and gentlemanly and took her to Madison Square Garden horse shows.
76.ch: New Orleans bands, Louis and the Lyric
76.q: But it didn't mean anything to Zutty because that was his life. He liked it. As I say, he liked the finer things in life, you see people always pick..... 125.t: Admired musicians' habits and Thompson's early drinking
125.s: He admired Waller, Calloway, Ellington and Hopkins as clean-cut, disciplined men, and says he was a professional drinker by 18.
125.ch: Moving, Columbia Missouri and leaving home
125.q: And as I said at this time there was Waller, Cab Calloway, Duke Ellington, Claude Hopkins. There's a difference between Claude Hopkins and Claude Thornhill, who comes later in my life. But they were all of these great musicians who looked up to and you admired

455.t: Hilton Jefferson: drinking buddy, Cab's punishing feature numbers
455.s: Hinton asks Budd about colleagues, and Budd praises Hilton Jefferson, whom Cab would test with hard features when he was drunk.
455.q: He was such a gentleman and quiet like, you would have to be with him a long time, like you did, really to know this man, I guess.

13.t: A congenial big band: the Wet and the Dry
13.s: No fights; drinkers vs. pot smokers.
13.ch: Swing, singers, Ed Fox and recordings
13.q: Yeah, family-type thing. It was a surprisingly congenial band to be as large as it was, 16 pieces, you know, 16 men. No arguments, fights, nothing, the whole time I was with the band.
